quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This means persuading someone to do something they were hesitant about.
quests.explanation: 'Talk someone into (something)' means to persuade them to do something they were initially unsure about. Notice the pronoun 'her' sits between 'talk' and 'into' — a separable pattern you've seen with other verbs.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically moved into anything — the phrase describes changing someone's mind through conversation.
quests.contextSentence: Even though she wasn't sure about skydiving, her friends eventually talked her ___ trying it.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence — the opposite persuasion from the phrase above.
quests.hint: This means persuading someone not to do something they were planning to do.
quests.explanation: 'Talk someone out of (something)' means to persuade them to abandon a plan, the reverse of 'talk into.' Together, these two phrases form a natural pair describing opposite directions of persuasion.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically moves out of anything — the phrase describes changing someone's mind against an existing plan.
quests.contextSentence: He wanted to quit his job on the spot, but his wife talked him ___ it.

quests.instruction: Choose the particle that fits the meaning in this context — read the whole sentence carefully before deciding.
quests.hint: Read the full sentence: despite not wanting to go, the person ended up going anyway.
quests.explanation: This tests careful reading rather than just the first clause. Although the speaker 'didn't want to go,' the phrase 'anyway' reveals that Sarah's persuasion succeeded in getting them to attend, which points to 'into,' not 'out of.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: the whole situation, not just one clause, determines the correct meaning here — a hallmark of more advanced reading comprehension.
quests.contextSentence: I really didn't want to go to the party, but Sarah talked me ___ it anyway.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb in this passive-voice sentence.
quests.hint: This describes an event being cancelled, expressed here in the passive voice.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'call off' in the passive voice — 'was called off' — inside a longer sentence with two clauses. The particle stays the same regardless of whether the sentence is active or passive; only the verb form changes.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — nothing is literally called anywhere — the phrase simply means the event was cancelled.
quests.contextSentence: Even though hundreds of people had already bought tickets, the outdoor concert was called ___ due to the incoming storm.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb in this sentence using a modal of deduction.
quests.hint: This describes a probable explanation for a delayed meeting, using a modal expressing likelihood.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'put off' inside the structure 'must have been put off,' a modal of deduction about the past. Recognizing the particle inside more complex verb structures like this is a key intermediate-level skill.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — nothing is physically pushed away — the phrase compares delaying an event to pushing it into the future.
quests.contextSentence: The meeting must have been put ___ because nobody showed up at the usual time.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb in this present-perfect sentence.
quests.hint: This describes someone finally stopping an effort, expressed with the present perfect tense.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'give up' in the present perfect — 'has given up' — describing a decision with ongoing relevance to the present moment (she's now calling a mechanic instead).
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — nothing is physically given away — the phrase describes surrendering an effort.
quests.contextSentence: She has finally given ___ trying to fix the old car herself and called a mechanic instead.

quests.instruction: Select the correct phrase to complete the sentence.
quests.hint: This means admiring someone and treating them as a role model.
quests.explanation: 'Look up to someone' means to admire them and treat them as an example to follow, the opposite attitude of 'look down on,' which you learned earlier. The two phrases form a natural pair describing very different kinds of regard for another person.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no one physically looks upward at another person — the phrase compares admiration to looking toward someone positioned above you.
quests.contextSentence: Ever since he was a boy, he has looked ___ his older brother as a role model.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence — the opposite attitude from the phrase above.
quests.hint: This means treating someone as inferior, the opposite of admiring them.
quests.explanation: 'Look down on someone' means to regard them as inferior, the opposite of 'look up to.' The clue here is people judging others unfairly based only on job title, a classic example of misplaced superiority.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no one is physically looking downward — the phrase compares feeling superior to literally looking down from above.
quests.contextSentence: Some people mistakenly ___ others just because of their job title.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence — read the full sentence carefully, including the phrase 'even after.'
quests.hint: This means continuing to admire someone despite a scandal, not losing respect for them.
quests.explanation: The phrase 'even after the scandal' signals that admiration continued despite bad news, which points to 'look up to,' not 'look down on.' This kind of clue — a full clause rather than one obvious word — is typical of more advanced reading.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: the phrase expresses ongoing admiration for someone, even when others might expect it to fade.
quests.contextSentence: Even after the scandal, many fans still ___ him.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This means understanding something with difficulty, often because of poor sound or sight quality.
quests.explanation: 'Make out' means to perceive or understand something with difficulty, often due to poor sound quality, bad handwriting, or low visibility. It's about sensory difficulty, not reasoning through a problem.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically 'made' — the phrase describes struggling to perceive something clearly through the senses.
quests.contextSentence: The recording was so noisy that I could barely make ___ what she was saying.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrasal verb that best completes the sentence — this is about perceiving something visually through difficulty, not reasoning through a problem.
quests.hint: This means visually perceiving something despite poor conditions, like fog or darkness.
quests.explanation: 'Make out' fits perceiving something visually despite difficult conditions, like thick fog. 'Figure out' and 'work out' both involve reasoning to solve a problem, which isn't the same as simply managing to see something.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physical is constructed — the phrase describes just barely perceiving a shape through poor visibility.
quests.contextSentence: Through the thick fog, the sailors could just make ___ the shape of the lighthouse.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb in this sentence with a negative and a modal.
quests.hint: This means struggling to read something clearly, even with the right equipment.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'make out' inside a negative modal structure — 'couldn't make out' — describing a failed attempt to read small print, even with glasses on.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physical is constructed — the phrase describes difficulty perceiving small details clearly.
quests.contextSentence: Even with my glasses on, I couldn't make ___ the small print on the label.

quests.instruction: Select the correct phrase to complete the sentence.
quests.hint: This means beginning to suffer from an illness, usually a minor one.
quests.explanation: 'Come down with (something)' means to begin suffering from an illness, typically something minor like a cold or flu. The coughing all week is the clue pointing to the onset of illness.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically descends — the phrase describes an illness beginning to take hold.
quests.contextSentence: She's been coughing all week — I think she's coming ___ a cold.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrasal verb that best completes the sentence — this is about recovering from an illness, the opposite direction from falling ill.
quests.hint: This means recovering after being sick for some time, the opposite of falling ill.
quests.explanation: 'Get over' means recovering from an illness, moving in the opposite direction from 'come down with,' which describes falling ill in the first place. The phrase 'after being sick for over a week' signals recovery, not onset.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nobody physically climbs over anything — the phrase compares recovering from illness to moving past an obstacle.
quests.contextSentence: He finally got ___ the flu after being sick for over a week.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct phrase to complete the sentence — this uses a modal describing a possible future outcome.
quests.hint: This means possibly beginning to feel ill in the future, if a warning isn't heeded.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'come down with' using the modal 'might end up,' describing a possible future consequence of poor sleep habits, rather than a fact already happening.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically descends — the phrase describes the possible onset of illness as a consequence.
quests.contextSentence: If you don't get more sleep, you might end up coming ___ something nasty.

quests.instruction: Select the correct phrase to complete the sentence.
quests.hint: This means finally finding the time to do something you've been intending to do for a while.
quests.explanation: 'Get round to (something)' means to finally find time for a task you've been meaning to do, often after a long delay caused by being busy rather than deliberately avoiding it.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically moves in a circle — the phrase describes finally reaching a task on your mental list.
quests.contextSentence: I've been meaning to fix the fence for weeks, but I never seem to get ___ it.

quests.instruction: Choose the particle that best completes the sentence — compare this with 'get round to,' which is about lack of time rather than active avoidance.
quests.hint: This means actively delaying something, often because of fear or reluctance, not simply lacking time.
quests.explanation: 'Put off' suggests active avoidance, often due to fear or discomfort, unlike 'get round to,' which usually implies simply not having had time yet. The mention of being scared is the clue pointing to deliberate avoidance.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — nothing is physically pushed away — the phrase describes deliberately delaying something uncomfortable.
quests.contextSentence: He kept putting ___ the dentist appointment because he was scared.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct phrase to complete the sentence — notice the time clause describing how long the delay lasted.
quests.hint: This means finally getting to a task after a long, unplanned delay.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'get round to' with an added time clause — 'by the time... three weeks had already passed' — emphasizing just how long an unplanned delay can stretch on, a natural feature of everyday spoken English.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically moves in a circle — the phrase describes finally reaching a task after unintentional delay.
quests.contextSentence: By the time she finally got ___ replying to his email, three weeks had already passed.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this 'put off' means losing interest, not postponing an event.
quests.hint: This means making someone lose interest or appetite for something, a different sense from postponing an event.
quests.explanation: 'Put someone off (something)' can also mean to make them lose interest or appetite for it, quite different from the 'postpone' meaning taught earlier. The unpleasant smell is the clue pointing to lost appetite here.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically pushed away — the phrase describes a sudden loss of enthusiasm or appetite.
quests.contextSentence: The strange smell in the kitchen really put me ___ eating there again.

quests.instruction: Choose the particle that best completes the sentence — this is the familiar 'postpone' sense from earlier.
quests.hint: This means rescheduling an event to a later time, the more familiar sense of this phrase.
quests.explanation: This reviews the original 'postpone' sense of 'put off,' rescheduling a barbecue because of rain — a useful contrast with the 'lose interest' sense taught earlier in this level.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase compares rescheduling an event to shifting it later on the calendar rather than cancelling it.
quests.contextSentence: We had to put ___ the barbecue because of the rain.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this uses the 'lose interest' sense with a group as the object.
quests.hint: This means causing a group of people to lose enthusiasm for a decision, because of someone's behavior.
quests.explanation: This reinforces the 'lose interest' sense of 'put off' with a new object — an entire hiring panel losing enthusiasm because of rude comments during an interview.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically pushed away — the phrase describes a group's enthusiasm fading because of someone's behavior.
quests.contextSentence: His rude comments during the interview put the panel ___ hiring him.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This means taking care of a task yourself so someone else doesn't have to worry about it.
quests.explanation: 'See to (something)' means to take responsibility for handling a task, often reassuring someone else that they don't need to worry about it.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally seen — the phrase describes taking personal responsibility for a task.
quests.contextSentence: Don't worry about the dishes — I'll see ___ them later.

quests.instruction: Choose the particle that best completes the sentence.
quests.hint: This means helping someone get through a difficult period, especially financially, until things improve.
quests.explanation: 'Tide someone over' means to help them manage through a difficult period, especially a financial one, until a better situation arrives, such as payday.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, borrowing the image of a rising tide carrying something safely through a rough patch until it passes.
quests.contextSentence: This small loan should tide us ___ until payday.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence — compare this with 'deal with' and 'sort out' from earlier in the curriculum.
quests.hint: This means personally taking charge of resolving a specific complaint.
quests.explanation: 'See to' fits personally taking charge of a specific matter, similar in spirit to 'deal with' and 'sort out' from earlier, but often used when someone is making a reassuring personal promise, as a receptionist might to a customer.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally seen — the phrase describes personally taking responsibility for resolving an issue.
quests.contextSentence: The receptionist said she would see ___ my complaint personally.

quests.instruction: Select the correct phrase to complete the sentence.
quests.hint: This means being alert to a specific danger or hazard nearby.
quests.explanation: 'Watch out for (something)' means to stay alert to a specific danger, such as a loose step, so you can avoid it. It's a common, friendly way to warn someone about something nearby.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: you genuinely keep your eyes open for a specific hazard.
quests.contextSentence: Watch ___ that step, it's a bit loose.

quests.instruction: Choose the particle that best completes the sentence.
quests.hint: This means waiting for a short moment, in a casual, spoken way.
quests.explanation: 'Hang on' is a casual, spoken way of saying 'wait a moment,' very close in meaning to 'hold on' but slightly more informal, often used with friends rather than in professional settings.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally hanging — the phrase simply means to pause briefly before continuing.
quests.contextSentence: Hang ___ a second, I just need to grab my keys.

quests.instruction: Choose the particle that best completes the sentence — very close in meaning to 'hold on,' but slightly more casual.
quests.hint: This means waiting briefly, in a relaxed, conversational tone.
quests.explanation: This reinforces 'hang on' as a close, more casual synonym of 'hold on.' Both mean to wait briefly, but 'hang on' feels more natural among friends or in relaxed spoken conversation, like checking a calendar together.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase simply asks someone to wait a short moment.
quests.contextSentence: Could you hang ___ while I check the calendar?

quests.instruction: Choose the correct phrase to complete this conditional sentence — read carefully, since the grammar here is more complex than usual.
quests.hint: This means someone was persuaded not to resign, expressed through a hypothetical past condition.
quests.explanation: This revisits 'talk out of' inside a past conditional structure — 'if... hadn't talked him out of... he might have quit.' The double negative logic (hadn't talked him out of resigning) confirms that his colleagues successfully prevented the resignation.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes persuading someone to abandon a plan, here embedded in a hypothetical past scenario.
quests.contextSentence: If his colleagues hadn't talked him ___ resigning, he might have quit on the spot.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence — a review of the admiration cluster from earlier in this file.
quests.hint: This means continuing to admire someone's early choices, despite everything that has happened since.
quests.explanation: This revisits the LOOK UP TO / LOOK DOWN ON contrast from earlier in this file. The phrase 'despite everything that happened' signals ongoing admiration rather than newly formed disrespect, pointing to 'look up to.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase expresses ongoing respect and admiration, even amid controversy.
quests.contextSentence: Despite everything that happened, the interns still ___ their mentor's early career decisions.

quests.instruction: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence — a fun, very natural idiom for describing total misunderstanding.
quests.hint: This means completely misunderstanding a situation, often in an almost opposite way from what was actually meant.
quests.explanation: 'Get the wrong end of the stick' means to completely misunderstand a situation, often in a way that's the near-opposite of the truth. It's a vivid, very natural idiom often heard in everyday spoken English, exactly the kind of full-situation understanding this stage of your learning has been building toward.
quests.correctAnswer: THE WRONG END OF THE STICK
options: THE WRONG END OF THE STICK
THE WRONG SIDE OF THE COIN
THE WRONG PART OF THE STORY
THE WRONG END OF THE ROPE
quests.literalVsFigurative: Fully figurative: no actual stick is involved — the phrase compares total misunderstanding to grabbing the wrong end of an object.
quests.contextSentence: He thought he was being fired, but he'd completely got ___ — it was actually a promotion.
